articles.title: Delhi Spent Years Wanting the Diaspora's Remittances. Now It Wants Its Portfolio.
articles.excerpt: A new RBI deposit scheme and the rise of GIFT City are reframing overseas Indians from senders of money home into investors in India — on terms built to compete with Dubai and New York.
articles.image_caption: Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City), India's tax-neutral financial hub courting NRI capital
articles.nri_angle: Overseas Indians are being courted with hedged, leveraged double-digit returns and tax-efficient GIFT City products that let them treat India as a serious portfolio allocation rather than just a place to send remittances.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Forbes Named America's 250 Most Successful Immigrants. Twenty-Six Are Indian.
articles.excerpt: Timed to the US's 250th anniversary, the list reads like a diaspora scoreboard — and quietly maps both how far Indian-Americans have climbed and where they still haven't.
articles.image_caption: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, one of 26 Indian-origin leaders on the inaugural Forbes 250 immigrants list
articles.nri_angle: The Forbes immigrant list is a measure of how thoroughly the Indian diaspora has woven itself into the top of the American economy — and an instruction, for a community fond of measuring itself, on the boardrooms and offices it still hasn't cracked.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Quiet Clause in the India-UK Trade Deal That Puts Money Back in Diaspora Payslips
articles.excerpt: From 15 July, a Double Contribution Convention ends the double social-security charge on Indian professionals posted to Britain — the human core of a deal usually sold on tariffs.
articles.image_caption: Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, in London for talks ahead of the India-UK trade pact rollout
articles.nri_angle: For the thousands of Indian professionals rotated through British client sites, the Double Contribution Convention ends years of paying into a UK pension they would never collect — a small, specific win for the diaspora inside a sweeping trade pact.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Diaspora's Money Is Pouring Home at Record Levels. It's Also Quietly Changing Shape.
articles.excerpt: India will take in nearly $140 billion in remittances this year. The bigger story is the shift from Gulf wages to Western capital — and how Delhi is racing to court it.
articles.image_caption: AMISOM Public Information via flickr (CC0)
articles.nri_angle: For 18.5 million Indians abroad, sending money home is shifting from obligation to investment — and India is now pricing the bond with competitive interest rates, equity caps and property rule changes aimed squarely at the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A 23-Year-Old and His Mother Just Became Mayors a Week Apart. Both Still Teach Hindi on Weekends.
articles.excerpt: Tushar Kumar and Parveen Rani's back-to-back Hertfordshire mayoralties are a feel-good headline — and a window into how the diaspora's British political climb now runs through the council chamber.
articles.image_caption: A civic building in London, where Indian-origin councillors are steadily taking on mayoral and council roles
articles.nri_angle: Britain's 1.9-million-strong Indian community is building political power from the ground up — in town halls and civic chains — and the Kumar-Rani story captures the second-generation balancing act of staying rooted while serving a chosen country.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Every Summer, 10,000 Telugu-Americans Fill a Convention Center. It's Not Really About the Concert.
articles.excerpt: From TANA in Dallas to ATA in Baltimore, the diaspora's convention circuit has become the load-bearing infrastructure of a community trying to keep its language alive one generation at a time.
articles.image_caption: A Bharatanatyam dancer in traditional attire, the kind of classical performance that anchors diaspora cultural conventions
articles.nri_angle: The biennial Telugu conventions are an organised answer to the second-generation problem every immigrant community faces — how to pass on a language and culture that the home country can no longer enforce from 12,000 km away.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Has Quietly Rewritten the Rulebook for Its 4.5 Million OCI Holders. Here's What Changed.
articles.excerpt: A new digital e-OCI system, a USD 275 fee for fresh cards, a hard three-month deadline to update your record after a new passport, and the death of the old PIO card add up to the biggest shake-up of the scheme in years.
articles.image_caption: An Indian passport; India has overhauled the rules tying OCI cards to a holder's current passport
articles.nri_angle: The OCI card is the document that keeps roughly 4.5 million people of Indian origin connected to India — visa-free entry and the right to live and work there — and the 2026 overhaul raises fees, kills the old PIO card, and imposes a hard three-month deadline (with a penalty) to update the record after every new passport, hitting frequent flyers, overseas students and mixed-passport families hardest.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Forty-One Years On, the Diaspora Still Gathers for Air India 182. The State Mostly Doesn't.
articles.excerpt: On June 23, families lit candles from Stanley Park to Ahakista for the 329 people killed in the world's deadliest act of aviation terrorism before 9/11 — a grief that built Canada's South Asian community and a justice it never received.
articles.image_caption: The Air India Flight 182 memorial at Humber Bay Park East in Etobicoke, Toronto
articles.nri_angle: The 1985 Air India bombing killed 268 Canadians, most of them of Indian origin, and remains the deadliest terror attack in Canadian history — a foundational wound for the Indo-Canadian community, whose families have spent four decades organizing memorials and fighting the perception that their dead were treated as a foreign tragedy rather than a Canadian one.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Indian-Australians Give Generously. A New Study Wants to Know Why So Little of It Is Counted.
articles.excerpt: Now the largest overseas-born group in Australia, the community gives out of faith, family and duty — but mostly outside the formal channels that track, deduct and amplify philanthropy. Researchers think that is a missed opportunity worth measuring.
articles.image_caption: Performers play traditional drums at an Indian community cultural festival
articles.nri_angle: Indians are now the largest overseas-born community in Australia, yet their considerable charitable giving is largely invisible to the formal philanthropic sector because it flows through temples, family networks and remittances home rather than registered foundations — a gap a new research effort aims to map, with implications for how the diaspora's wealth shapes both Australian causes and India.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Europe Is Quietly Courting Indian Students — and Seeding the Diaspora's Next Chapter
articles.excerpt: The EU has awarded 75 Indians Erasmus Mundus scholarships and launched a student ambassadors' network, building the connective tissue that turns student flows into settled communities.
articles.image_caption: International students at a European university (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Where students go is where communities eventually form. Europe's deliberate recruitment of Indian talent is the early signature of diaspora clusters that do not yet fully exist — as old America-or-Britain defaults loosen.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Prince William Just Gave Two Young Indians the Diana Award's Top Honour. Neither Lives Abroad.
articles.excerpt: An 18-year-old who built a power-cut-proof bulb and a 24-year-old mental-health campaigner were among 20 worldwide winners of the Diana Legacy Award, handed out in London.
articles.image_caption: Prince William, the Prince of Wales, who presented the Diana Legacy Awards in London
articles.nri_angle: For a community that prizes recognition abroad, two young Indians being honoured on a British stage by a future king — for solving Indian problems on the world's terms — is the diaspora's soft power at its purest.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Sunday Panel in Manhattan Showed What the Indian-American Community Actually Worries About Now
articles.excerpt: GOPIO's free 'College and Beyond' session put an AI engineer and a Hindi teacher on the same stage — a quiet bid to widen the diaspora's definition of a respectable career.
articles.image_caption: A community panel discussion; Indian-American leaders gathered in Manhattan to weigh the diaspora's current concerns (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Volunteer-run community organisations are transmitting hard-won knowledge of the American higher-education maze to the diaspora's next generation — a sideways form of giving back that the CEO-and-Congress headlines miss.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Indian-Australians Mark 12th International Day of Yoga From Canberra to the Gold Coast
articles.excerpt: Diplomatic missions and community groups staged synchronised events nationwide, with this year's healthy-ageing theme resonating for a maturing diaspora.
articles.image_caption: Participants gather for an outdoor group yoga session marking International Day of Yoga.
articles.nri_angle: Shows how Australia's large and increasingly organised Indian community turned International Day of Yoga into a nationwide soft-power and community-building event.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: President Murmu Courts Indian Communities in Portugal and Slovakia on Europe Tour
articles.excerpt: A two-nation visit, including the first by an Indian head of state to Slovakia in 29 years, widens New Delhi's diaspora diplomacy across the EU.
articles.image_caption: President Droupadi Murmu, who toured Portugal and Slovakia to meet the Indian diaspora.
articles.nri_angle: Examines how India is extending its diaspora outreach to smaller European states, addressing the 125,000-strong Indian community in Portugal and a small but growing population in Slovakia.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: GOPIO Connecticut Marks 20 Years, Honours Five Leaders and Gives $50,000 to Charity
articles.excerpt: A two-decade-old diaspora chapter shows how Indian-American immigrant networks are maturing into permanent civic institutions.
articles.image_caption: A speaker addresses the GOPIO-CT 20th anniversary banquet in Darien, Connecticut.
articles.nri_angle: Chronicles how an Indian-American community organisation in Connecticut has evolved over 20 years into a durable civic institution, a model relevant to NRI communities across the United States.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: ‘On the Menu’: Indian-American Lawmakers Tell the Diaspora to Stop Watching and Start Running for Office
articles.excerpt: At a Capitol Hill event, three Indian-American congressmen warned that economic success no longer buys political protection, and urged the community to seek power at every level of government.
articles.image_caption: Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, who urged Indian-Americans to run for public office at a FIIDS event on Capitol Hill.
articles.nri_angle: For a first-generation diaspora that arrived to study and work, these lawmakers are asking the community to trade quiet, private success for visible political power as anti-India and anti-Hindu incidents rise.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Gulf Was the Diaspora's Safe Haven. A War Is Forcing 9 Million Indians to Recalculate.
articles.excerpt: As conflict reshapes West Asia, Indian community networks have become a quiet backbone of mutual aid, even as the divide between the diaspora's professionals and its labourers grows starker.
articles.image_caption: The Dubai skyline at dusk; nearly 3.5 million Indians live and work in the United Arab Emirates.
articles.nri_angle: The Gulf holds the largest single bloc of overseas Indians and a pillar of India's $135bn in remittances; the war is testing both their physical safety and the unspoken bargain that drew them there.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Diaspora With No Homeland to Return To Is Trying to Build One in the Cloud
articles.excerpt: As Sindhis gather in Toronto this July, the community is attempting something it has rarely managed in 70 years of dispersal: a permanent global institution to hold itself together.
articles.image_caption: Members of the South Asian diaspora gather at a community cultural event.
articles.nri_angle: The Sindhis run the assimilation experiment without the safety net of a homeland, making their fight to preserve language and identity an accelerated preview of what every Indian diaspora community eventually faces.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: How a Single Sunday of Yoga Maps Britain's Indian Diaspora
articles.excerpt: From a Jain centre in Hertfordshire to a square in Birmingham, the 12th International Day of Yoga showed the organizing muscle, and the soft power, of a community.
articles.image_caption: Participants take part in a mass open-air session marking the International Day of Yoga.

sources.label: IANS — Indian missions worldwide mark International Day of Yoga
Oshwal Association of the U.K. — International Yoga Day 2026
United Nations — International Day of Yoga 2026

articles.nri_angle: Britain's coordinated Yoga Day celebrations reveal the Indian diaspora as both the original carrier of yoga to the West and a living infrastructure of community organizations now deploying it as cultural diplomacy.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: On Long Island, a Parade Becomes a Measure of How Far Indian-Americans Have Come
articles.excerpt: The curtain raiser for the 15th India Day Parade drew 250 people and a row of elected officials, evidence of a diaspora moving from enclave to mainstream.
articles.image_caption: Indian-Americans celebrate Independence Day with a flag-raising procession in New York.

sources.label: The Indian EYE — 15th India Day Parade USA 2026: Curtain Raiser Draws A Full House
The Indian EYE — IDP USA India Day Parade of Long Island

articles.nri_angle: The Long Island India Day Parade shows how a maturing Indian-American community converts cultural celebration into political visibility, while wrestling with how to pass its volunteer-built institutions to a second generation growing up American.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: In a Paris Concert Hall, Modi Recasts the Diaspora as India's Ambassadors Abroad
articles.excerpt: Addressing overseas Indians at the Salle Pleyel, the prime minister offered affection and a quiet argument: that the community is now an instrument of national influence.
articles.image_caption: Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a visit to France, where he addressed the Indian diaspora.

sources.label: The Indian EYE — PM Modi lauds diaspora as true strength of India-France ties
IANS — PM Modi given warm welcome by Indian diaspora in Paris: MEA
IANS — Paris is city of lights and colours: PM Modi to Indian diaspora

articles.nri_angle: Modi's Paris address crystallizes how his government has recast overseas Indians from emigrants who left into strategic 'Rashtradoots' expected to carry India's trade, technology and image into their adopted countries.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ottawa and Delhi Barely Spoke for Two Years. This Week, 100 Companies Flew In to Change That.
articles.excerpt: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal led India's largest-ever business delegation to Canada — and cast the Indo-Canadian diaspora as the bridge that outlasted the diplomatic freeze.
articles.image_caption: Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, who led the largest-ever Indian business delegation to Canada
articles.nri_angle: After two years caught in the India-Canada diplomatic crossfire, 1.8 million Indo-Canadians are being recast from a security headache into the relationship's most valuable asset as trade talks revive.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Stretch of the Jersey City Waterfront Vanished Under Colored Powder. For Thousands, It Was the Only Holi They Know.
articles.excerpt: Surati Holi Hai 2026 drew thousands to Exchange Place — a summer-scheduled spring festival that shows how the diaspora keeps tradition alive by replicating the feeling, not the calendar.
articles.image_caption: Revelers covered in colored powder at a Holi festival celebration
articles.nri_angle: For second-generation kids who have never seen Holi in India, the Jersey City festival is not a copy of home — it is the real thing, and the institution-building behind it is what turns a population into a community.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Taste of Home Used to Arrive in a Suitcase. Now It Has a Shelf in the Duty-Free Hall.
articles.excerpt: Premium Indian beverages have entered Canada's airport duty-free retail — a milestone built, one grocery run at a time, by 1.8 million Indo-Canadians.
articles.image_caption: An airport duty-free retail hall, where premium Indian products are now finding shelf space
articles.nri_angle: The generation that arrived with spice boxes wrapped in newspaper now watches its children pass Indian brands in the duty-free hall — the pantry that once marked them as outsiders has become a category the mainstream wants to sell.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Diaspora Famous for Sending Money Home Just Pledged $1 Million to Feed Americans Instead
articles.excerpt: The HungerMitao movement, built on the slogan 'give where you live,' is quietly redirecting Indian-American philanthropy toward the country the community actually lives in.
articles.image_caption: Volunteers pack food donations at the Capital Area Food Bank in the U.S. (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: HungerMitao reframes who the diaspora is responsible for — arguing an Indian-American shares a moral claim with a hungry neighbour in their own US city, not only with causes back in India. It is both a unifying force across a fragmented community and a statement of belonging.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Cricket Legend and a Blind Industrialist Walked Into a Charity Gala. The Diaspora Opened Its Wallet.
articles.excerpt: At the Sankara Eye Foundation's annual fundraiser, Sunil Gavaskar's autographed bats and Srikanth Bolla's life story turned nostalgia into surgeries for the blind back in India.
articles.image_caption: Former India captain Sunil Gavaskar, who headlined the Sankara Eye Foundation's diaspora fundraising gala
articles.nri_angle: Diaspora philanthropy that funds free eye surgeries in India shows how NRI giving has institutionalised — audited charities, celebrity draws, named sponsor tiers — as a way for immigrants to stay tethered to home and pass that obligation to American-raised children.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Each Summer, a Building-Sized Chariot Rolls Down a North American Street. That's the Whole Point.
articles.excerpt: The Ratha Yatra has become the diaspora's most outward-facing ritual — staged on public streets from New York to Vancouver, designed for the neighbours who have never set foot in a temple.
articles.image_caption: Devotees pull a towering chariot during an ISKCON Ratha Yatra procession
articles.nri_angle: Unlike inward-looking diaspora gatherings, the Ratha Yatra is staged in public for a non-Indian audience — inverting the exclusivity of the Puri original, doing cheap and effective soft-power work, and giving American- and Canadian-raised children a sensory link to a tradition their parents left behind.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two American Doctors Got One of India's Highest Honours This Week. Both Left India Decades Ago.
articles.excerpt: At the second Padma investiture of 2026, President Droupadi Murmu pinned the Padma Bhushan on a New York radiation oncologist and the Padma Shri on a Kansas gastroenterologist — a reminder that India still counts the diaspora's achievements as its own.
articles.image_caption: Dr Dattatreyudu Nori receiving a Padma award at a Civil Investiture Ceremony at Rashtrapati Bhavan; the New York radiation oncologist was conferred the Padma Bhushan in 2026
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin doctors are one of the diaspora's biggest contributions to the West — a huge share of physicians in the US and UK — yet they rarely get formal recognition from the homeland; pinning a Padma Bhushan and a Padma Shri on two American-based physicians is India publicly counting the medical diaspora's success as its own, and telling emigrant families that a foreign passport and decades abroad don't cut the tie.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Britain's Big India Summit Left London This Year. It Went to the Midlands Instead.
articles.excerpt: The 10th UK-India Week opened at the University of Warwick, with a Gujarat delegation courting West Midlands leaders on investment, skills and clean energy — a sign that the diaspora's economic diplomacy is moving out of the capital and into Britain's industrial heartland.
articles.image_caption: The University of Warwick in the West Midlands, which hosted the opening of the 10th UK-India Week in 2026
articles.nri_angle: Britain's largest concentration of Indian-origin families and businesses sits outside London, in places like the West Midlands; moving UK-India Week's regions forum to the University of Warwick — and pairing a Gujarat delegation with Midlands leaders — is an attempt to turn the diaspora's informal, decades-old family and professional networks into formal investment pipelines, university tie-ups and clean-energy and manufacturing deals.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Diaspora Has Spent 20 Years Collecting Trophies. India Just Handed It a Database Instead.
articles.excerpt: At a New Jersey gala for Indian-American achievers, the Consul General launched a free trade portal — and asked the room for its address book, not its cash.
articles.image_caption: The global spread of the Indian diaspora, now the world's largest
articles.nri_angle: The India-USA Trade Facilitation Portal reframes the diaspora's economic role: not remittances, but using its knowledge of American markets to connect small Indian exporters with US buyers as part of the $500bn Mission 500 trade target.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Says NRIs Can Buy Its Mutual Funds. For Indians in America and Canada, Most Fund Houses Say No Anyway.
articles.excerpt: The barrier isn't Indian law — it's FATCA. Only eight to ten of India's 44 fund houses will onboard US and Canadian NRIs, pushing the diaspora's richest cohort toward GIFT City workarounds.
articles.image_caption: The Bombay Stock Exchange building on Dalal Street, Mumbai
articles.nri_angle: The US and Canadian diaspora — India's wealthiest and most courted overseas communities — are the ones most often locked out of Indian mutual funds, because FATCA compliance costs make AMCs refuse them. A structural exclusion built into the diaspora's tax status.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Has a Museum for Almost Everyone. A Group of Indian-Americans Is Tired of the Gap.
articles.excerpt: After eight years validating 11,000 years of history, the team behind the India Heritage Center wants a $14 million permanent home for India's story in the US capital.
articles.image_caption: The National Mall in Washington; Indian-Americans are pushing for a museum to mark their place in the American story
articles.nri_angle: A second-generation anxiety made physical: as Indian-Americans reach the center of US life, they worry their children are losing the connection to India's history. The India Heritage Center is a bet that a permanent museum in Washington can hold that thread.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
